title: The Dual Coding Delusion
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that dual coding theory, as originally proposed by Allan Paivio and later operationalised by Richard Mayer and John Sweller, has been reduced in schools to the crude mantra "add pictures to your teaching," losing the mechanism that made it work in the first place. He explains that dual coding only benefits learning when visual and verbal information are complementary, integrated, cognitively economical, and generative -- not merely present together -- citing Mayer's modality, coherence, contiguity, and signalling principles as the conditions under which combining words and images helps rather than hinders. Using worked examples of a mislabelled heart diagram and a Macbeth soliloquy paired with an unrelated image, he shows how split attention and misalignment between word and image can overload working memory and actively undermine the schema-building dual coding is meant to support. He closes by arguing that the danger isn't using visuals, but forgetting what they're for: a visual should carry meaning that words alone make harder to see, not decorate a slide.
points: Didau's central historical corrective is important: Paivio's dual coding was a descriptive theory of memory representation, never a prescriptive classroom instruction to "add pictures" -- that translation happened later, and imperfectly, through Mayer and Sweller's applied principles.

His four "active ingredients" for dual coding to work -- complementarity, integration, cognitive economy, and generativity -- give teachers a checklist for evaluating whether a visual is actually doing cognitive work or just decorating a slide.

The mislabelled heart-diagram and Macbeth-soliloquy examples both illustrate the same underlying failure mode (split attention or misalignment between word and image), showing the theory breaks the same way across very different subjects.

Didau's closing diagnosis names a specific classroom pathology -- the "visual Esperanto" of generic clip-art icons (lightbulb for "idea," handshake for "agreement") -- as evidence of the theory's mechanism being lost while its surface form spread unchecked through CPD culture.
quotes: But as with so many ideas in education, what began as an elegant theory has metastasised into caricature.

Crucially, though, dual coding was never intended as an instruction manual. It was a descriptive theory of how information might be represented in memory, not a prescriptive guide to classroom practice.
In classroom life, dual coding has been simplified into add pictures to your teaching. This is roughly equivalent to saying that because protein builds muscle, you should eat steak for every meal.
If words and images pull in different directions, or if graphics are merely decorative, the extra channel becomes noise rather than signal.
Teachers, in an earnest bid to dual code, raid sites like the Noun Project, pasting generic icons as if clip-art could stand in for cognition.
The danger of over-simplified dual coding lies not in using visuals, but in forgetting what they’re for.
